sources.news_title: UK police release five on bail over air base incident
sources.text:
British police said on Monday five men arrested near an air base used by the United States were released on bail, as officers probed whether a "foreign state" could be involved in a suspected bomb plot.
US President Donald Trump, speaking in Washington, said he was "surprised that they released them," adding that "I wouldn't have done that."
The release of the five – all London-based Britons in their mid-20s – came as British Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced an emergency meeting of top officials to ensure they have "the full picture."
Earlier, Iran had denied involvement in any plot to target the Royal Air Force (RAF) Fairford base in Gloucestershire, south-west England, following the security scare there early on Sunday.
UK counter-terror police are leading the investigation after authorities received reports on Sunday of three "suspicious" white vans near the air base, which has been used by the US to bomb Iran.
Police said in their latest update on Monday that the five men held, who all live in inner London boroughs, were being released on bail.
"This does not mean the investigation is over," Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, the head of Counter Terrorism Policing, said, adding the five would be subject to "stringent" bail conditions.
He said officers were "considering this from every possible angle, including that this may be activity committed by proxies, or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly, working on behalf of a foreign state."
The men were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and "preparation of a terrorist act" under UK anti-terrorism laws, according to police.
They had been travelling in the three suspect vehicles, which have since been subject to "extensive examination, with the support of military assets and forensic experts."
Amid huge questions about what happened, authorities have not confirmed any details of the threat, but bomb-disposal experts were seen at work at the scene.
The Daily Mail and Press Association both reported late on Monday they understood from sources that tests on materials in the back of the vans established they were "not viable explosives."
A farmer living in the village of Whelford near the air base said she rang the police after seeing the vans blocking a road and a group of masked men.
The anonymous woman told media on Monday that she believed the police had "dropped the ball" on the threat.
But UK defence minister Wes Streeting said she only had a "partial picture."
Trump on Sunday said the UK and US had the suspects "under investigation" for a while and alleged "they were looking to do big damage to our fort."
On Monday, after hearing news of their bail, Trump said the case "might be" linked to Iran but declined to elaborate.
Pressed to give details, Trump said: "I'd rather not. I mean I know the answer, I could be very specific, but I'd rather not say. I would not have released them."
Iran's embassy in London said on X that it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" speculation that Tehran was involved.
It criticised "the recent unfounded and malicious speculations published by some British individuals and media outlets attempting to link Iran" to the incident.
In March, Britain gave the US permission to use Fairford for "specific defensive operations into Iran" to destroy Iranian missiles at source.
Since then, US bombers and other planes have been seen taking off and landing from the base – the only one on Britain's mainland used for this purpose.
Residents in the rural Cotswolds area surrounding Fairford said the site, which hosts a range of US military equipment and personnel, had seen increased activity and security in recent months.
Around 85 households were evacuated from the village early on Sunday, and had to stay elsewhere overnight, but were allowed back to their homes late on Monday.
Tehran has previously warned London against allowing its bases to be used by the US in operations against Iran.
In March, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi accused London of "putting British lives in danger" by allowing the bases to be used "for aggression against Iran." (AFP)
Edited by Cecil Wong

5 men arrested near U.S. bomber base in Britain released on bail
Five men arrested on suspicion of preparing a terrorist attack near a British air base used by U.S. bombers have been released on bail, according to British authorities. They remain under investigation, with strict restrictions on their movements and contact with others.
The men were released on Monday afternoon following extensive interviews and inquiries, according to Laurence Taylor, the head of Britain’s counterterrorism police. They were arrested early Sunday near RAF Fairford, a Royal Air Force base in Gloucestershire in southwestern England.
“To be very clear, this does not mean the investigation is over,” Taylor said. “They absolutely remain under investigation as we explore multiple lines of enquiry.”
Armed officers arrested the men in nearby Whelford after police received a report at about 12:45 a.m. on Sunday of three suspicious vehicles traveling toward the base. They were initially held on suspicion of explosives offenses and later on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act.
Military personnel and forensic experts examined the three vehicles overnight. The Sun reported that material found inside what it described as three white vans was “not viable explosives.”
Residents who were evacuated from about 85 households have now been allowed to return home, according to Gloucestershire Police. A cordon remains around the vehicles as investigators continue their work.
“I’m surprised that they released them. I wouldn’t have done that,” Trump told reporters at the White House. “We know everything about them. We would have not released them.”
Trump said on Sunday that the men were “looking to do big damage” to the base. Sky News had also reported that investigators were examining a possible Iranian connection.
There has also been speculation that the men may have been involved in a fuel-stealing operation, but authorities have not confirmed that account.

sources.news_title: Five Men Arrested Near RAF Fairford Released on Bail as Police Examine Possible Foreign-State Link
sources.text:
Five men arrested near RAF Fairford after a report of suspicious vehicles have been released on police bail, but remain under investigation on suspicion of explosives and terrorism offences, counter-terrorism police said on Monday.
The men, all British nationals aged between 23 and 25, were detained in Whelford, Gloucestershire, early on Sunday. Armed officers responded after police received a report that three vehicles were travelling towards the nearby airbase. Investigators have spent the intervening hours examining the vehicles with military and forensic support, while residents of about 85 households were evacuated as a precaution. They have since been told they can return home, although a cordon remains around the vehicles.
The arrests have prompted an investigation with international implications because RAF Fairford is a major operating location for American bombers. Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, the head of Counter Terrorism Policing, said detectives were considering several explanations, including whether anyone involved had acted, knowingly or otherwise, on behalf of a foreign state. He did not identify a state or say that investigators had established such a connection.
Police have disclosed no finding about what the men intended to do, whether the vehicles contained explosives or whether the airbase was their intended target. None of the five has been charged.
Taylor said the decision to grant bail followed extensive interviews and inquiries. The men remain subject to conditions restricting their movements and contact with others, he said, and detectives continue to pursue multiple lines of inquiry. Police have not published the precise bail conditions.
The five are London residents. According to Counter Terrorism Policing, three live in Westminster, one in Camden and one in Willesden. The Westminster residents are 23, 24 and 25; the other two are 24. Police initially arrested them on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act and subsequently on suspicion of preparation of a terrorist act under Section 5 of the Terrorism Act. Those are grounds for investigation, not findings of guilt.
A late-night sighting in Whelford
The incident began in the countryside immediately east of RAF Fairford. Gloucestershire Constabulary said it received a call at about 12.45 a.m. on Sunday concerning three suspicious vehicles travelling towards the base. Armed officers responded and arrested the five men in the Whelford area. By Sunday morning, police had declared a major incident and the Army’s explosive ordnance disposal specialists were examining the vehicles. Officers established a cordon of about 400 metres, and residents from roughly 85 households were advised to leave.
A local farmer gave a more personal account of how the alarm was raised. She told the BBC that, on arriving home, she found three white vans blocking her driveway and the road and saw a group of hooded and masked men. Some ran into a field and others towards neighbouring Kempsford, she said. After an unanswered call to Ministry of Defence police at the base, she said she called 999 at 1.36 a.m. and saw armed officers arrive within about 10 minutes. She believes her call disrupted whatever the men were doing.
Police have not publicly reconciled their stated time of the first report, 12.45 a.m., with the farmer’s account of a 1.36 a.m. emergency call. Nor have they established publicly whether her call alone led to the arrests. Her account describes what she saw and did; the sequence of all information available to officers remains part of an incomplete public picture.
The farmer later questioned why she had received no follow-up from authorities and said she had seen enough to know something was unusual. Gloucestershire Police’s temporary chief constable, Maggie Blyth, responded to broader questions about the police operation by saying officers had acted appropriately and quickly on calls made to them. She thanked local people for the information they had provided.
The evacuation sent some residents to friends and relatives and others to a leisure centre opened for those needing shelter. Police said on Monday evening that households could return, while the area immediately around the vehicles remained closed to allow investigators to continue their work. Blyth acknowledged the anxiety and disruption in communities that had suddenly drawn international attention, and said some questions could not yet be answered without affecting the investigation or security.
For the village, the easing of the evacuation did not mark the end of the operation. Officers and specialist teams remained at the scene on Monday. Taylor said all three vehicles had undergone extensive examination overnight with assistance from military assets and forensic experts. Police have not announced the results of those examinations.
Why the airbase has drawn attention
RAF Fairford is a British airbase used by the United States Air Force. The U.S. Air Force describes it as its preferred forward operating location in Europe for Global Strike Command bombers. Its 420th Air Base Squadron supports deployed forces and flying operations there. The base’s role gives the investigation a significance beyond the surrounding villages, even though police have yet to establish publicly what the suspects were doing near it.
American bombers have used Fairford during the conflict involving Iran, under a British policy permitting the United States to use British bases for operations the government describes as defensive. In July, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps warned that bases used for attacks on Iranian territory would be treated as legitimate targets. That history explains the scrutiny of a possible foreign-state connection; it does not establish one in this case.
Iran’s embassy in London rejected speculation linking the country to the Fairford arrests, calling it unfounded and malicious. Taylor, for his part, said investigators were keeping an open mind about whether the wider geopolitical situation had any bearing on events in Whelford. He said detectives were examining the possibility of activity by proxies or people acting for a foreign state, including people who might not know whose interests they were serving. theguardian.com
That is a line of inquiry, not an announced conclusion. As of Monday night, police had disclosed neither evidence tying the five men to Iran nor evidence tying them to any other government. They had also not identified a group, published a suspected motive or said an attack had been imminent. Counter Terrorism Policing said it was still working to establish the men’s activities, knowledge and possible motivation.
The investigation has reached the highest levels of government. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he would chair a Cobra meeting on Monday to review the situation. He urged against speculation while authorities established the facts. The meeting came as police, the Ministry of Defence and local agencies continued work at the scene and supported displaced residents. t
President Donald Trump criticised the bail decision during remarks in Washington, saying he was surprised the men had been released and that he would not have done so. Trump also said the United States and Britain had worked closely together on the matter. British police have not publicly detailed any U.S. role in the investigation or explained their evidence in enough detail to assess the president’s criticism of the bail decision.
Trump had earlier suggested the men had been under scrutiny for some time. British officials have not publicly confirmed the scope or timing of any surveillance. For the farmer who reported the scene in Whelford, that claim sharpened questions about what authorities knew before the vehicles were spotted. The police account released so far describes the call and the armed response, but does not provide a full chronology of any earlier intelligence.
The decision to release the men on bail leaves detectives able to continue investigating while imposing restrictions on them. Taylor was emphatic that bail had not closed the case. His statement offered no timetable for a charging decision or for the removal of the remaining cordon.
By Monday evening, Whelford residents had permission to go home, but investigators were still working around the three vehicles that brought armed police to the village. The central questions remained open: what was in the vehicles, what the five men intended, and whether anyone beyond them had a part in the incident. Police said their examination of the scene and wider inquiries were continuing.

The US president said he was “surprised that they released them” and claimed American law enforcement would not have done so.
The five British nationals were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and terrorism on Sunday after three suspicious vans were found near RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, which is used by the US.

Andy Burnham chaired a meeting of the government’s emergency Cobra committee to discuss the incident on Monday afternoon.
Afterwards, defence secretary Wes Streeting said: “We’re acutely aware that the events at RAF Fairford have caused considerable disruption to the local community and also wider public concern.

sources.news_title: Trump Criticizes UK Bail Release After RAF Fairford Arrest
sources.text:
President Trump said he was surprised five British suspects walked free on bail after a terror scare near a U.S.-used air base, and made plain he would not have released them.
Five British men from London, ages 23 to 25, were arrested in the early hours near RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire after three vans loaded with barrels of material were found about 350 metres from the base. Armed officers moved in fast. Homes were cleared. Tests later indicated the material was not viable explosives. By afternoon, Britain’s top counter-terrorism officer confirmed the men were out on police bail, still under investigation, still under conditions, but free to leave custody.
Trump did not hide his reaction. He said he was “surprised” the five had been released and added he would “not have done so.” The president also praised the joint work that led to the arrests, telling reporters the suspects had been under view and were looking to do serious harm to what he called “our fort.”
The episode left a village on edge, a major investigation open, and a blunt gap between American bluntness and British process in plain view.
A local farmer returning home found three white vans blocking the road and driveway near Whelford. She saw a group of hooded and masked men. When they spotted her, they ran, some into a field, some toward the neighboring village of Kempsford.
She first tried the Ministry of Defence police line. No answer. At 1.36 a.m. she dialed 999. Within about ten minutes, she said, the village filled with armed officers. The men were rounded up quickly. Officers stripped them amid fears they might be wearing suicide belts. Arrests began under the Explosives Act and moved onto terrorism charges.
Eighty-five homes were evacuated. Residents later returned, but a cordon stayed around the three vehicles. Gloucestershire Police and Counter Terrorism Policing kept the scene locked down while bomb disposal and investigators worked the vans.
Reuters reported a roughly 400-metre cordon and said a source familiar with the inquiry viewed an Iranian-linked motive as the most likely track under review, with other angles also examined. Police have not closed the case or named a final theory.
Landing comments and follow-ups put the White House squarely in the story. Trump said the suspects had been known and watched. “We know all about them. You’ll be hearing about it very soon. We caught them,” he said. He called the cooperation with Britain “fantastic” and “an amazing job,” adding the group was “looking to do big damage to our fort.”
He also said the men had been “under view for a long time.” On the bail decision itself, his verdict was short and clear: surprise, and a statement that he would not have cut them loose that way.
Breitbart noted the base’s role hosting U.S. bombers in Middle East operations and reported British investigators were examining a possible Iran link without declaring a finished state-backed plot. Heightened hostile-state activity involving Iran proxies has been a live concern for UK security services.
Outside New Scotland Yard, Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, Britain’s senior counter-terrorism officer, put the release on the record. “I can confirm that, following extensive interviews and inquiries, the five men who were arrested are being released on police bail this afternoon,” he said.
Taylor stressed the limits. “To be very clear, this does not mean that the investigation is over. They are subject to stringent conditions on their movement and contact with others.” He added: “They absolutely remain under investigation as we explore multiple lines of enquiry.”
Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans, Counter Terrorism Policing’s senior national coordinator, called it a large, complex operation involving local and national policing, the Ministry of Defence, and local agencies. She thanked armed officers who arrived not knowing what they would face and asked for space to work without a rush to judgment on motive.
“I am very aware of the levels of speculation about the motivation behind this incident and the geopolitical questions being raised,” Evans said. “However, I ask that Counter Terrorism Policing be given the space at this time to carry out its work carefully and thoroughly.”
Overnight searches produced multiple new lines of inquiry, police said. Hostile-state involvement and proxies remain among the angles under review. Officials also left room for other explanations, including decoy activity. No final public finding has pinned the barrels, the vans, or the five men to a completed attack plan.
Iran’s London embassy “categorically rejects” any involvement and called circulating claims “unfounded and malicious speculations.” The embassy statement framed the coverage as fuel for what it called Iranophobia and reserved the right to legal steps over what it labeled misleading narratives.
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, speaking after a Cobra emergency meeting, said police and security services had moved rapidly to contain the situation. He praised the farmer’s quick action while noting she had only a partial picture. “We are making no assumptions about the background and motivation of the arrested individuals,” Streeting said. He also defended the U.S. presence at Fairford: “Having the US at Fairford makes us more safe, not less safe. Be in no doubt about that.”
The five men are all British and from London, three linked to Westminster, one to Camden, and one to Willesden in Brent. Full names have not been released. The Daily Mail reported that tests on the seized material established it was not viable explosives, even as the vans stayed inside a police cordon and the inquiry continued.
Resident Laura Stitt, 40, voiced the frustration many felt when the temperature dropped so fast. “The main concern is it has been de-escalated very quickly from being potential terrorism,” she said. She also objected that the arrested men appeared able to head toward home before some locals could fully settle back into theirs, and she pointed to the heavy spend of police time and taxpayer money amid lingering confusion.
The farmer who made the 999 call pushed back on official talk that she lacked the full picture. “I know it’s been said by some of the higher ups today that I didn’t have the full picture, but the picture I had was three extremely unusual vehicles parked in the middle of our village and a group of unknown men running around,” she said. She added that no one in official capacity had followed up with her even after she gave her number to 999.
She described the base on high alert, civilian staff already moved, and her shock that a member of the public spotted the vans first. “A plucky amateur shouldn’t be spotting unusual activity at 1am when the air base is on high alert,” she said. “I think it’s absolutely astonishing.” She also said police knew about the vans after her call yet did not evacuate until around 6 a.m., leaving homes near the vehicles exposed in the gap.
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage tied the episode to a wider warning. “If a farmer coming home from a party at 1am is the person that discovered these people, it does raise questions,” he said. Farage argued Trump was saying more in public about the security picture than Britons were hearing at home, and he claimed the country faces “cells” of enemies inside its borders. “Trump saying what he says verifies my worst fears,” Farage said.
What remains settled is narrow and serious. Five men were seized near a base used by American forces. Three vans and barrels of material triggered a major armed response and the evacuation of 85 homes. Counter-terrorism police say the men stay under investigation with strict bail limits on movement and contact. Iran denies any hand in it. Trump says the group was watched, caught, and aimed at doing major damage, and he would not have sent them out on bail.
What remains unsettled is larger. Motive is not locked down. The exact nature of any hostile-state or proxy role is still under review. The public still lacks full names, full charging detail, and a complete account of how long the men had been watched versus how much turned on a farmer’s late-night drive home. SAS troops were reported deployed from Hereford as the scene locked down. MI5 and counter-terrorism units stayed in the hunt for who stood behind the scare.
British officials ask for patience and space. American leadership calls the result a success and the bail call a mistake. Taxpayers in a quiet Gloucestershire village got the raid, the evacuation, the cordon, and then the sight of suspects walking out under conditions while questions still hang over a base that hosts U.S. power projection.
When a president says the suspects were hunted, caught, and bent on big damage, turning them loose on bail is not caution, it is a choice the public will judge against the next threat that does not miss.

Bell explained that under normal circumstances, "the U.S. and U.K. governments would carefully coordinate to make sure their messaging was entirely in line in such situations."

sources.news_title: Five British Nationals Released on Bail as RAF Fairford Terror Investigation Expands
sources.text:
By yourNEWS Media Newsroom.
LONDON — Five men arrested near RAF Fairford over the weekend have been released on police bail after extensive questioning, even as British counterterrorism officials stressed that the suspects remain under investigation and that authorities are pursuing several possible explanations, including potential involvement by a foreign state.
The men are all British nationals, ages 23 to 25, and residents of London, according to information released Monday by Counter Terrorism Policing and reported in BBC coverage of the investigation. Police have not publicly released their names, ethnicities, birthplaces, immigration histories or any information indicating whether they hold additional nationalities.
Three of the suspects are 24 years old, while the others are 23 and 25. Police said three live in Westminster, one in Camden and one in Willesden.
Head of Counter Terrorism Policing Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor announced Monday afternoon that all five would leave custody following questioning.
“I can confirm that following extensive interviews, and inquiries, the five men who were arrested are being released on police bail this afternoon,” Taylor said.
“To be very clear, this does not mean the investigation is over, they are subject to stringent conditions on their movement and contact with others. They absolutely remain under investigation as we explore multiple lines of inquiry. At counter-terrorism policing we are working within this context every day and we are keeping an open mind in this investigation.”
Police have not charged any of the five men.
The suspects were initially arrested early Sunday under Britain’s Explosives Act after police received a report at approximately 12:45 a.m. concerning three suspicious vehicles apparently traveling toward RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire. They were subsequently arrested on suspicion of preparing an act of terrorism under Section 5 of the Terrorism Act.
RAF Fairford is owned by the United Kingdom but has long served as an important operating location for the U.S. Air Force. American B-1 and B-52 bombers have operated from the base during this year’s conflict with Iran, making the installation strategically significant to both countries.
Counterterrorism investigators have not concluded that Iran, Russia or any militant organization directed the alleged activity.
Taylor said Monday that authorities were examining whether the suspected offenses might have involved “proxies or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly working on behalf of a foreign state.”
“I know there is significant interest in whether the current geopolitical context has a bearing on this incident,” Taylor said.
“We are considering this from every possible angle. Including, that this may be activity committed by proxies, or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly, working on behalf of a foreign state,” he added.
A source familiar with the inquiry told Reuters that investigators have examined an Iranian-linked motive along with the possibility of Russian-directed sabotage or activity connected to a non-state militant group. Those remain investigative theories rather than established conclusions.
Iran has denied any involvement.
The Iranian Embassy in London said in a public statement that it “categorically rejects” and “strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations published by some British individuals and media outlets” connecting Iran with the incident.
“The circulation of such fabricated speculations, particularly in the aftermath of the criminal acts of aggression committed by the United States and the Israeli regime against the Iranian people, will serve no purpose other than to fuel Iranophobia propaganda in the UK,” the embassy said.
“The Islamic Republic of Iran reserves the right to take appropriate legal measures, as necessary, to safeguard the rights and interests of the country and its people in response to misleading and damaging media narratives,” it added.
The investigation began not with an announced counterterrorism raid but after a member of the public reported suspicious activity near the base.
A local farmer told the BBC that she encountered a “large group of hooded and masked men” around three vans parked near Whelford in the early hours Sunday.
She said the men appeared alarmed when she approached.
In a separate account given to The Telegraph, the woman said: “I saw a group of Middle Eastern-looking young guys running off through the trees. Some of them had masks or balaclavas on, and they all scattered ahead of us as we drove back past… Some of them ran into the fields, and some of them turned to run towards the air base. We realised this was something pretty serious.”
The description reflects the witness’s account; police have not publicly disclosed the ethnicity of any of the five arrested men.
The farmer said police arrived rapidly after she called emergency services.
“I still can’t process how that base, on high alert, how this has happened… I think it was pure luck that I arrived in the village at a similar time to the vans,” she said. “I’m absolutely staggered that it was left to me, as a member of the public, to see and report this.”
Reuters reported that a source familiar with the investigation said the arrests were not “intelligence-led,” although security around RAF Fairford had already been increased because of the wider threat environment.
That account has raised questions because President Donald Trump said Sunday that U.S. and British authorities had been monitoring the men.
Trump said the suspects had been “under view for a long time and we got them.”
“We had them under investigation. They were looking to do big damage to our fort, and working with the British worked out great,” Trump said.
The apparent difference between Trump’s description and the public account of the farmer’s emergency call has prompted questions about whether authorities already knew of a potential threat but were not specifically tracking the three vans.
British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting suggested Monday that additional intelligence exists but said he could not discuss operational details.
“I do want to thank the member of the public who acted quickly and called this in,” Streeting said. “I would also just say, respectfully, that she has a partial picture… And I won’t go beyond that, in terms of commenting on operational security matters.”
Streeting declined to publicly connect the suspected plot to Tehran.
Asked about Iran, he said he was not “drawing a connection with Iran,” while adding that British authorities are aware of threats involving Iran and its proxies.
Police initially established a 400-meter security cordon around the three white vans and evacuated approximately 85 households in Whelford while military explosive-ordnance specialists and forensic teams examined the vehicles. A bomb-disposal robot was used during the operation.
Taylor said Monday that all three vans had undergone extensive examination and that substantial police resources remained deployed at the scene.
Britain’s Press Association separately reported, without identifying its sources, that investigators had not found viable explosives. Police had not publicly confirmed that report as of Monday afternoon.
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood later said the scene had been made safe through the work of the Army’s explosive ordnance disposal team and that evacuated residents could return home.
The limited information released about the suspects has generated political demands for greater disclosure.
Police have confirmed only their British nationality, ages and London areas of residence. British nationality establishes citizenship but does not disclose where a person was born, whether citizenship was acquired at birth or later, whether someone has dual nationality or their ethnic background.
Reform UK deputy leader Richard Tice called for authorities to disclose additional information, including whether any of the suspects were dual nationals, had an asylum history, were previously known to law enforcement, had criminal convictions or were receiving public assistance.
No official evidence released Monday established any of those circumstances.
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage also criticized the government’s handling of national-security threats, telling the BBC that Britain needed to take the issue more seriously.
“We have allowed into Britain cells of people who intend to do us harm,” Farage said.
However, police have not said the five suspects entered Britain from abroad, were members of an established terrorist cell or shared any particular immigration history. The only nationality information publicly released is that all five are British nationals.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he would chair a meeting of the government’s COBRA emergency committee Monday afternoon to obtain a wider assessment of the case.
“I want to thank the police, the Gloucestershire Police, the security services, the emergency services, the public who alerted us, so thank you to everybody for the way that they’ve worked,” Burnham said.
“What I can say is that I will chair a meeting of Cobra later this afternoon just to make sure we have the full picture, the full situation very clearly in our sights and so maybe we’ll say more about that later today.”
Liberal Democrat MP Roz Savage, whose South Cotswolds constituency includes the area around Fairford, also called for clarification about the apparently different descriptions offered by Trump and British authorities.
She said there appeared to be “two incompatible accounts.”
“The president (Donald Trump) is saying this was all coordinated, but it seems people here and on the ground and local police were not aware of a joint intelligence operation. These are the answers that we absolutely have to get,” Savage said. “It actually makes my blood run cold when I think how close we may have come to disaster this weekend.”
Authorities have not yet publicly explained whether Trump’s statements referred to intelligence collected before Sunday’s events, a broader investigation already underway or information obtained after the farmer’s call.
The possibility of foreign-state involvement has drawn particular attention because of RAF Fairford’s role in U.S. military operations.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said in July that military installations used in attacks against Iranian territory could be considered legitimate targets. RAF Fairford has hosted U.S. bombers involved in Middle East operations during the current conflict.
Britain has also reported increasing Iranian-linked national-security activity in recent years.
In a separate case earlier this month, British counterterrorism police arrested two people on suspicion of assisting a foreign intelligence service in an investigation explicitly linked to Iran. Both were later released on bail with conditions pending further investigation.
Those previous cases provide context for why investigators are examining an Iran connection at Fairford, but they do not establish that the five men arrested Sunday were acting for Tehran.
The U.S. Air Force said personnel at RAF Fairford “remain vigilant” but declined to discuss specific security procedures “for operational security reasons.” The U.S. Embassy in London has also advised Americans in Britain to remain cautious and mindful of their personal security.
Monday’s decision to release the five suspects on bail significantly changes their immediate legal status but does not end the inquiry.
British police can impose bail conditions while investigators continue collecting forensic, digital and intelligence evidence. Taylor said the five men face restrictions on their movements and contact with other people.
The investigation therefore remains open on several fundamental questions: what the men intended to do, what was inside the vans, whether additional people were involved, whether any foreign government or organization had a role and what British or American intelligence agencies knew before the arrests.
Police have also not publicly provided evidence establishing the men’s ethnicity, place of birth, immigration status, dual-nationality status, political or religious affiliations, criminal histories or source of income.
For now, the confirmed picture is narrower: five British nationals from London were arrested near a strategically important air base, questioned on suspicion of explosives and terrorism offenses, then released under strict bail conditions while one of Britain’s most significant current counterterrorism investigations continues.

The current position is that five suspects are on bail and remain under investigation, while authorities continue to establish what happened near RAF Fairford. Any decision on further arrests, charges or no further action will depend on the evidence gathered.

Five British men arrested over a suspected terror plot near a UK air base could have been close to launching a “sophisticated” attack on the site, a former police counter-terror chief has warned.
Counter-terror police today released the men, who are in their 20s and from London, on bail after they were arrested with suspected explosives near RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire on Sunday.
Laurence Taylor, head of National Counter Terrorism Policing, said one line of enquiry is whether individuals may have been working unknowingly on behalf of a foreign state.
Shorts
The i Paper understands they had been under surveillance for some time, but that the arrests were opportunistic rather than the result of direct intelligence.
Meanwhile, security concerns have been raised over how close the masked suspects were able to get to the key air base without police or security services seemingly being aware.
A farmer who raised the alarm after spotting three vans and masked men near the site on Sunday morning told The i Paper she believes she saw around eight or nine suspects – and criticised police for only evacuating locals several hours after she alerted 999.
What kind of attack could have been planned?
Early indications suggest any plan to target the base, which is used by US and British air forces, may have included “a level of sophistication that isn’t common in terrorism”, a former counter-terror chief told The i Paper.
Nick Aldworth, an ex-detective chief superintendent in counter terrorism policing, said the fact that vans featured fake company branding in an apparent bid to avoid raising suspicion and the alleged targeting of a military airfield suggested detailed planning likely to be beyond self-radicalised terrorists.
Aldworth added that the arrangement of the three vans at the time of the arrests suggested preparations were under way to unload the vehicles.
He said: “It appears that the vehicles were parked in a way that suggests to me separation for unloading. You can see the way they’re all positioned with their doors in that sort of little fan shape – and then people away from the vehicles rather than in them and driving.
“The important thing is if those people that were arrested were not with those vehicles at the point of arrest. First priority is going to be to try and tie them into those vehicles because you know the obvious defence is, ‘Not my vehicle boss.’
“A really important investigative plan at the moment will be to actually confirm that the people who’ve been arrested were associated with those vehicles and with whatever might be in those vehicles.”
What planes could have been targeted?
RAF Fairford has been used by US aircraft involved in the air campaign against Iran. Any attack on the base, would be fraught with difficulty.
Its runway is almost two miles long and is reinforced to support heavy bombers such as the B-1 Lancer and B-52 Stratofortress, and also hosts a detachment of U-2 high-altitude reconnaissance aircraft, said Chris Bergs, an air power analyst at think tank the Royal United Services Institute (Rusi).
“Fairford provides reserve capacity, and the ability to quickly fold in significant US striking power when required. This can be used to send a clear signal to adversary nations,” he said.
Ministry of Defence (MoD) police as well as armed US personnel patrol the base, which is “a significant political and deterrent asset”, added Bergs.
It was “very hard” to see how a plan to crash through the gates in a van, and place a vehicle next to a plane before fleeing, could succeed, said Aldworth.
“Maybe there’s the possibility of them having a number of small devices in those vans. And the plan was to take small devices out, try and break through the fence, and then place devices against aeroplanes,” he suggested.
“I don’t think that would be a viable plan because, while these perimeters are big and hard to protect, the assets inside them are more commonly protected. Particularly, the Americans would generally have an armed guard on an aeroplane like that.”
Police ‘took hours to evacuate locals’
People living nearby said security at the site had been ramped up in the days before the incident, with tractors and concrete pillars appearing to have been positioned at entry gates to block access at the start of last week.
The farmer who raised the alarm after spotting three vans and masked men near RAF Fairford in the early hours of Sunday said she believes there were “at least eight or nine” suspects at the scene.
The local resident, who wished to remain anonymous, said she called 999 after there was no response when she rang an emergency number for the Ministry of Defence (MoD) police.
“We think we saw at least eight or nine,” she told The i Paper.

The men were detained early Sunday after three vans were spotted in the countryside near RAF Fairford, a U.K.-owned base that has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East, including this year’s war with Iran.
Taking questions from reporters on a variety of topics at the White House on Monday, President Trump said he would not have released the men.
Investigators haven’t concluded whether the incident was state-backed. They are investigating a possible link to Iran, Russia or non-state militant groups. RAF Fairford has also been the focus of protests by anti-war campaigners.
The five suspects, who haven’t been named, were initially held over suspected explosives offenses, and later also arrested on suspicion of preparing an act of terrorism. Police said the men are all British nationals from London and in their 20s.
Britain’s national news agency, PA, reported without citing sources that police had not found viable explosives. Announcing that the suspects had been bailed, the head of U.K. Counter Terrorism Policing, Laurence Taylor, said that the suspects face stringent conditions and “absolutely remain under investigation.”
Taylor said lines of inquiry include that the suspected offenses were committed by “proxies or individuals, either knowingly or unknowingly, working on behalf of a foreign state.”
Iran denied involvement. The Iranian Embassy in London said that it “categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations” about the incident.
Residents were evacuated from 85 homes in the village of Whelford near the base Sunday, and army bomb-disposal experts used a robot to examine three white vans. The villagers were allowed to return home late Monday afternoon, though a cordon remained around the three vehicles, police said.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham chaired a meeting of the government’s COBRA emergency committee on Monday “to make sure we have the full picture” of the incident, he said.

British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting said the farmer “did exactly the right thing” by calling police but had only “a partial view” of the operation.
The arrests came at a time of heightened tensions around the threat from hostile states, with British intelligence services saying Russia and Iran have both used proxies to commit crimes on U.K. soil. In March, officials said the number of national security cases involving activity by hostile states, including Iran, increased by 50% in the six months leading up to December 2025.
Iran has been linked to a series of attacks in Europe
Britain didn’t join the U.S. and Israel in the Iran war, which began on Feb. 28, and initially denied Trump’s request to use bases in the U.K. to strike Iran. But then Prime Minister Keir Starmer agreed in March to let the U.S. use bases in Britain for what he called “defensive” operations against Iran’s missiles and their launch sites following Iranian attacks on U.K. interests and Britain’s allies in the gulf.
American B-1 and B-52 bombers have taken off from Fairford, 100 miles west of London, for operations during the Iran conflict.
Iran has said that it considers any base used to attack its territory a legitimate target.
British security officials say proxies linked to Iran have been behind a string of arsons and other attacks in the U.K. and other countries, many of them targeting the Jewish community and intended to sow fear. They have previously warned that Tehran could expand its targets in the U.K. if conflicts in the Middle East continue.
Several people also have been charged with plotting to commit arson in the U.K. on behalf of Russia-linked groups.
U.K. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said Monday that the incident is a “reminder of the threats our country faces.”
Miliband met Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi at the United Nations in New York last week and told him that “Britain will not tolerate intimidation, threats or hostile activity on U.K. soil,” according to a U.K. readout of the conversation.
U.S. Air Force says personnel remain vigilant
The U.S. Air Force said that its personnel on the base “remain vigilant,” but “for operational security reasons we will not discuss specific force protection measures.”
The U.S. Embassy in London has warned Americans in Britain to be cautious and mindful of their personal security.
Trump said that authorities had the suspects “under view for a long time and we got them.”
“It was an amazing job. We had them under investigation. They were looking to do big damage to our fort. And working with the British worked out great,” he told reporters in Chicago on Sunday.

sources.news_title: 5 Men Released On Bail After Arrest Near U.S.-Run Air Base In England, Police Say
sources.text:
FAIRFORD, England (AP) — Five young British men arrested on explosives and terror charges near a U.S.-operated air force base in England were released on bail on Monday, and counterterror detectives said they were investigating “multiple lines of inquiry,” including whether there is a link to Iran.
The men were detained early Sunday after three vans were spotted near RAF Fairford, a U.K.-owned base that has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East.
Investigators haven’t concluded whether the incident was state-backed. They are investigating a possible link to Iran, Russia or non-state-backed militant groups. RAF Fairford has also been the focus of protests by anti-war campaigners.
The five suspects, who haven’t been named, were initially held over suspected explosives offenses, and later also arrested on suspicion of preparing an act of terrorism. Police said that the men are all British nationals from London and in their 20s.
The head of U.K. Counter Terrorism Policing, Laurence Taylor, said that the suspects face stringent bail conditions and “absolutely remain under investigation as we explore multiple lines of inquiry.”
Iran denied involvement. The Iranian Embassy in London said that it “categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations” about the incident.
Residents were evacuated from 85 homes in the village of Whelford near the base on Sunday, and army bomb-disposal experts used a robot to examine three white vans. The villagers hadn’t been able to go home as of Monday morning, and the vans hadn’t been moved yet.
The arrests came after reports of suspicious vehicles
U.S. President Donald Trump said the suspects had been detained following cooperation between the U.S. and Britain, and had been “under view” for some time. Police, however, said the arrests were triggered by a late-night call about “suspicious vehicles” near the base.
U.K. Defense Secretary Wes Streeting declined to give details of the operation, but said that “it was a proud moment” that Trump had recognized “the work that our police and intelligence services do every day.”
“As and when we can, we will report back to the public about these individuals and about the nature of the threat,” Streeting told Times Radio.
The arrests came at a time of heightened tensions around the threat from hostile states, with British intelligence services saying Russia and Iran have both used proxies to commit crimes on U.K. soil. In March, officials said the number of national security cases involving activity by hostile states, including Iran, increased 50% in the six months to December 2025.
Iran has been linked to a series of attacks in Europe
Britain didn’t join the U.S. and Israel in the Iran war, which began on Feb. 28, and initially denied Trump’s request to use bases in the U.K. to strike Iran. But then Prime Minister Keir Starmer agreed in March to let the U.S. use bases in Britain for what he called “defensive” operations against Iran’s missiles and their launch sites following Iranian attacks on U.K. interests and Britain’s allies in the Gulf.
American B-1 and B-52 bombers have taken off from Fairford, 100 miles (160 kilometers) west of London, for operations during the Iran conflict.
Iran has said that it considers any base used to attack its territory a legitimate target.
British security officials say proxies linked to Iran have been behind a string of arson and sabotage attempts in the U.K. and other countries, many of them targeting the Jewish community. They have previously warned that Tehran could expand its targets in the U.K. if conflicts in the Middle East continue.
U.K. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said Monday that the incident is a “reminder of the threats our country faces.”
Miliband met Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi at the United Nations in New York last week and told him that “Britain will not tolerate intimidation, threats or hostile activity on U.K. soil,” according to a U.K. readout of the conversation.
U.S. Air Force says personnel remain vigilant
The U.S. Air Force said that its personnel based at RAF Fairford “remain vigilant,” but “for operational security reasons we will not discuss specific force protection measures.”
The U.S. Embassy in London has warned Americans in Britain to be cautious and mindful of their personal security.
Trump said that authorities had the suspects “under view for a long time and we got them.”
“It was an amazing job. We had them under investigation. They were looking to do big damage to our fort. And working with the British worked out great,” he told reporters in Chicago on Sunday.

Trump criticizes UK for releasing suspects in alleged terror plot targeting base used by US
By Nic Robertson, Tim Lister and James Frater CNN
Fairford, England (CNN) — US President Donald Trump criticized the United Kingdom’s response to a suspected terror plot to attack a UK airbase used by the US military, saying he was “surprised” the five suspects were released on bail on Monday afternoon.
Speaking to reporters in the Oval Office, Trump said he wouldn’t have released the suspects, suggesting their actions “might be” connected to Iran. But Trump refused to elaborate further, saying only: “I know the answer. I can be very specific, but I’d rather not say it.”
The release of the men does not mean that the investigation is over, and all five will be subject to stringent conditions on their movements, British counter-terrorism police said Monday.
Downing Street said it did not have an immediate response to Trump’s comments, and directed CNN to earlier statements made by police. Iran denied any involvement in the incident.
The men, who have not been identified, were arrested early Sunday close to the base at Fairford in western England, from where US B-1 bombers have been flying missions against Iran.
The five are all British nationals from the London area, aged between 23 and 25, according to counter-terrorism police.
Laurence Taylor, a senior counter-terrorism police officer, said the police were considering the incident from every possible angle, “including that this may be actively committed by proxies or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly working on behalf of a foreign state.”
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham chaired a meeting of COBRA – a committee that handles national emergencies – later Monday.
Interior minister Shabana Mahmood said that, as of Monday afternoon local time, “the scene is now safe.” A police cordon remains around three vehicles found at the scene.
About 85 households, who were evacuated from the area on Sunday, were told by police on Monday evening that they can return to their homes.
UK authorities have not disclosed where the men were detained, nor what was found in three white vans they appear to have used.
Aerial footage on Sunday showed a bomb disposal robot roaming between the vans in woods near the base. The rear doors of two of the vans were open and large black items could be seen scattered on the ground nearby.
CNN teams nearby later heard what sounded like two controlled detonations from the direction of the village where the vans were found.
Following the emergency committee meeting, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said that the investigations remain live, adding that “those five individuals are under stringent bail conditions.”
Iranian threat
Iran earlier denied any involvement in the incident. Its embassy in London issued a statement Monday saying it “strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations published by some British individuals and media outlets attempting to link Iran to arrest of five suspects in the vicinity of RAF Fairford base.”
The Iranian embassy has yet to comment on Trump’s remarks.
Asked if a hostile foreign state could have been behind the incident, British Defense Minister Wes Streeting said on Monday that he did not “want to speculate at this stage of the investigation.”
In July, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps specifically noted Fairford’s use by US bombers, warning the UK that “any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces.”
On Sunday, Trump called the arrests “fantastic,” saying the US and the UK had the men under investigation for “a long time.”
“Working with Britain, it was an amazing job,” Trump told reporters in Chicago. “They were looking to do big damage to our fort and working with the British worked out great.”
“We had them under view for a long time, and we got them,” he said.
UK authorities have not commented on that assertion. It’s unclear whether the five men were under surveillance before their arrival in the Fairford area in the early hours of Sunday.
“Hooded and masked”
Photographs of the men – shirtless with their hands tied behind their backs – appeared in UK media Sunday.
They were initially detained under laws on possession of explosives and were later additionally arrested “on suspicion of preparation of a terrorist act,” according to a statement by counter-terrorism police.
A local resident said she came across the men when returning home on Saturday night.
“Both the driveway and the road were blocked by three white vans,” she said.
The resident, who wishes to remain anonymous, told CNN that the vans were parked in a “strange formation” about 100 meters from the base fence.
She believed there were “definitely” more than five men in the group and most had their faces covered. However, authorities have not indicated they are looking for other individuals and said Sunday the situation had been contained. CNN is reaching out to police on the discrepancy.
Some ran into the field and some towards the neighboring village, the resident said.
She called the emergency services at 1:40 a.m., according to phone records she showed CNN. Within ten or 15 minutes, armed police arrived.
“I think it was pure luck that I arrived in the village at a similar time to the vans,” the resident, a farmer, added.
Multiple UK media outlets – including the BBC, the Guardian and the Telegraph – reported, citing sources, that the operation was not intelligence-led, suggesting the vigilance of local residents may have played a key role in alerting authorities.
Counter-terrorism police said they first received a call “relating to three suspicious vehicles which appeared to be travelling towards the airbase” about an hour before the resident made her emergency call.
Streeting said the resident had “a partial picture” of the situation, adding that the work of the police and the security services “takes place often unsung, unreported, for good reason,” he said.
Tightened security
Local people told CNN that security around the base had been tightened in recent days, with roadblocks at the entrance. But roads and lanes in the immediate area were still open.
The woman who called the police and one other local resident said that during previous conflicts, such as that against Iraq in 2003, there had been heavy security around the base.
But security since the Iran conflict began has been less evident, they said.
In March, the UK government gave the US Air Force permission to use Fairford to carry out strikes on Iranian missile sites used to attack ships in the Strait of Hormuz.
Days after the IRGC issued its threat against Fairford in July, Iranian media published a video of a group describing themselves as Iranian patriots at the perimeter fence of the base.
“This is RAF Fairford on British soil — the place where US military aircraft take off from these very runways to attack our people and our homeland,” one man says, with an Iranian flag hanging on the fence.
A US Air Force spokesperson at Fairford – where the 501st Combat Support Wing is based – told CNN on Sunday: “For operational security reasons we will not discuss specific force protection measures.”
CNN’s Molly English and Lauren Kent contributed to this report.

THE five men arrested over a potential terror plot near RAF Fairford are being released on police bail, head of Counter Terrorism Policing, Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, said.
The news was revealed in a press conference in London at around 3.40pm on Monday, September 27.
The five men arrested over a potential terror plot near RAF Fairford are being released on police bail, the head of Counter Terrorism Policing has said.
Assistant Commissioner Taylor told reporters outside New Scotland Yard: “I can confirm that following extensive interviews and enquiries, the five men who were arrested are being released on police bail this afternoon.
“To be very clear, this does not mean that the investigation is over.
“They are subject to stringent conditions on their movement and contact with others.
“They absolutely remain under investigation as we explore multiple lines of inquiry.”
Police are considering 'every possible angle' in their investigation into what happened at RAF Fairford including whether it was carried out by proxies or individuals working on behalf of a foreign state, Assistant Commissioner Taylor said.
Speaking at New Scotland Yard, Mr Taylor said he knows there is 'significant interest in whether the current geopolitical context has a bearing on this incident'.
Mr Taylor continued: “At counter-terrorism policing, we are working within this context every single day, and at this stage, we are keeping an open mind in this investigation.
“We have, as you would expect, ensured that our protective security advice and posture remain commensurate to the threat.
“But be assured, we are considering this from every possible angle, including that this may be actively committed by proxies or individuals, either knowingly or unknowingly, working on behalf of a foreign state.
“To respond to incidents such as these, rapid mobilisation is necessary, as we cannot take the risk whilst assessing that threat.
“However, once we understand the threat more clearly, we seek to return affected communities to normality as quickly as possible.
"We still have significant resources deployed at the scene.
"A cordon remains in place while investigators continue their work.
"However, we are hopeful to reduce this later today and get residents back to their homes and will provide further updates on this in due course.
"I know for the people who call this area and RAF Fairford home that this has been a hugely disruptive incident.
"I thank you for your support and for your patience."
"I would ask the public to remain vigilant and report anything suspicious to the police.
"I'm also very conscious that there is a great deal of speculation about what may or may not have been previously known about potential threats or activity.
"As I hope the public will understand, I will not always be able to share this type of information.
"What I do ask is that the public understand that we work hand in glove with MI5 to keep them safe from a myriad of threats and do everything we can to protect them.
"Incidents such as this are a reminder of the importance of public vigilance.
"If you spot something that doesn't feel right, please let us know."

sources.news_title: Two Bail Decisions: Fairford And Basingstoke - The Heartlands Tribune
sources.text:
Bailed and Remanded: What Fairford and Basingstoke Tell Us About Justice Before Trial
We were told a bomb plot had been foiled beside an American airbase in the Cotswolds. A day and a half later, the suspects were free, the cordon was shrinking and the public was left with nothing but briefings.
Two bail decisions came within a single week.
On Friday, a 37-year-old roofer named Daniel Thomas, known to his supporters as Danny Tommo, appeared at Basingstoke Magistrates’ Court. He pleaded not guilty to criminal damage after allegedly slashing a boat in the Channel with an emergency responder on board. He also denied refusing to give police the PIN to his phone. He was refused bail and sent to prison to await trial.
On Monday, five young men from London, arrested in the dead of night beside an RAF base used by American bombers, were released. They had been held on suspicion of Explosives Act offences and preparing a terrorist act. Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of Counter Terrorism Policing, told reporters outside New Scotland Yard that they were leaving custody on police bail under “stringent conditions”.
Many readers will look at those two outcomes and conclude the system has its thumb on the scale. The feeling is understandable. Honesty requires us to say the cases are not the same. Thomas has been charged, and a court judged whether he should wait for trial behind bars. The Fairford five have not been charged. Police released them because, for now, they either lack the evidence to charge or the grounds to ask a court for more time.
That distinction matters. It also opens a more troubling question than the one being shouted on social media.
WHAT WAS IN THE VANS?
On Sunday the country watched aerial footage of a bomb disposal robot circling three white vans near the village of Whelford. Two had their rear doors open. Large black objects lay scattered around them. Reporters near the perimeter fence heard what sounded like two controlled detonations. At least 85 homes were evacuated.
By Monday afternoon every suspect was walking free, the cordon was being scaled back and residents were being told they could go home. Police have still not said what, if anything, was in those vans.
Plenty of people will be exasperated by this, and they are entitled to be. For a day and a half the public was invited to believe that a serious bomb plot had been stopped on the edge of the Cotswolds. The authorities’ own conduct since then tells a smaller story. Suspects in a live plot to bomb an airbase are not usually back on the streets within 36 hours. Either the evidence is thinner than Sunday’s headlines suggested, or the state is asking us to trust it without showing why.
Either there was a viable explosive device, or there was not. The public is owed the answer.
If there was a working device, releasing five men without charge after so short a time is extraordinary, and ministers should explain it. If there was not, the country deserves to know why Sunday’s story looks so different by Monday. Bail in national-security cases is not unheard of: in a separate case, the husband of Labour MP Joani Reid and two other men were bailed after being arrested by counter-terrorism officers on suspicion of spying for China. What is unusual is the distance between the drama of the operation and the modesty of its result.
WHO HAS BEEN BRIEFING, AND WHY?
Before anyone had been charged, the Daily Telegraph reported that police are understood to suspect Iran as the most likely state actor. The Iranian Embassy in London “categorically” rejected the claim. Defence Secretary Wes Streeting then said the farmer who raised the alarm “had a partial picture”. She had tried the base’s own hotline, got no answer, dialled 999, and later told the BBC the authorities had “dropped the ball”.
Context matters here. In March, Keir Starmer, then Prime Minister, allowed US strikes on Iranian missile sites to be launched from Fairford. A government that has tied British soil to an American war has an obvious interest in a story about Iranian aggression on English soil. That does not make the story false. It means the story should be tested in a courtroom, not settled by anonymous briefings to friendly newspapers.
ONE LAW, FOR EVERYONE
The principled answer to Basingstoke is not to demand that the Fairford men be locked up. It is to insist on the same standard for everyone. The presumption of liberty before trial belongs to a far-right activist accused of slashing a dinghy and to five Londoners picked up near an airbase. Those who want the state to show its evidence in one case should want it in the other. The left forgot this once. The right is forgetting it now.
Thomas’s lawyers will apply again at Portsmouth Crown Court. The Fairford investigation continues. In both cases the question is the same, and it is the only one that should matter: what can the state prove?
Justice is judged on evidence, not headlines, and nobody should be jailed or cleared by press briefing.
